stances.claim: Amid the SC's internal crisis, the right response as a 'family elder' is to grieve, listen quietly, give private counsel to those who seek it, and pray -- not to moralize, mock, or justify publicly.
Reinhold Niebuhr's serenity prayer is the author's operative framework: courage to change what he can (private counsel), serenity to accept what he cannot, wisdom to know the difference.
The QW decision is not yet final -- the MR and the Senate resolution on QW are still pending -- justifying continued restraint.
Edgardo Angara was more than an outstanding lawyer, banker, educator, and statesman -- he was, in the author's personal experience, a humble, thoughtful, and caring friend.

decision_framework_signals: Apply the Niebuhr framework when facing institutional crises: categorize between what you can change (private counsel) and what you must accept
Choose silence as an active, principled decision rather than passive avoidance -- delicadeza as an institutional virtue

one_paragraph_summary: Faced with reader and media pressure to comment on the QW ouster of CJ Sereno (May 11, 2018), Panganiban explains his principled silence through Reinhold Niebuhr's serenity prayer: 'Lord, grant me the courage to change the things I can, the serenity to accept those I cannot, and wisdom to know the difference.' He frames himself as a 'family elder' in the SC institution -- and when a beloved family is wracked by internal dissension, excruciating pain, and serious crisis, the right response is to grieve, listen quietly, give private counsel to those who seek it, and pray, not to sermonize, mock, or justify. He cites delicadeza as barring him from disclosing the private conversations with incumbent colleagues, and notes that Cardinal Tagle texted from Bangkok on May 11 when the ouster broke -- the author replying briefly with a plea for a 'more extensive and balanced view' later; Tagle replied, 'Thanks po and we pray po.' He also notes the QW decision is not yet final (MR pending; Senate resolution on QW still to be resolved). He pivots to a tribute for the late Edgardo J. Angara ('EJA, Ed, Edong'), recounting their first meeting in 1979 when Angara was IBP president, his founding of the Asean Law Association in 1980 (of which the author is current Philippine chapter chair), the 1982 UP Oblation miniature from Angara, Angara's facilitation of an honorary UP Phi Kappa Phi membership, the January 2013 Gopac conference in Manila, the June 30, 2012 Baler event celebrating the 113th Siege anniversary and the 200th-Year Cadiz Constitution anniversary, and their Metrobank Foundation association. Against Sen. Zubiri's characterization of Angara as 'one of the best presidents we could have had,' the author chooses to remember him simply as 'a humble, thoughtful and caring friend.'
